              12 steps, from checking the car to packing away

              Follow these steps in order, one at a time. Under each step there is a 🧭 tag that tells you which idea the step uses and which level it comes from. If a step doesn’t pass, don’t skip ahead to the next one. Always go back and fix it first.

              1. Check the body first Upload the test code from Lesson 16 and put the car on a box so the wheels are off the ground. Check that drive() turns both wheels forwards. If a wheel turns backwards, swap that motor’s wires (the same way as in Lesson 16). Do this step before you upload the new code, because once you upload the new code, the old code is gone.

                🧭 The body must be ready before the brain can drive · Level 0

              2. Make 4 cards An up arrow, a left arrow, a right arrow and an open palm. Draw the arrows big and thick, almost filling the paper. Use a dark pen on light paper so the camera can see them more clearly.

                🧭 The classes are the answers the AI can choose from · Level 2

              3. Teach the eyes On Teachable Machine create an Image Project. Name the classes Forward Left Right Stop (it doesn’t matter if you use capital or small letters, or leave a space at the end of a name, but they must be these English words), then add a fifth class Nothing for an empty scene and any other objects, which the web page turns into S for you. Collect at least 50 pictures for each class: in bright and dim light, close up and far away, with several different people’s hands, in the room where you will really drive. Only photograph the cards or hands, never faces. Don’t press the flip button (it mirrors the picture). If you press it by accident, change the third argument of new tmImage.Webcam(224, 224, true) to false in the code. To edit the code, you need the files on your computer: download the kit zip, then edit ai-driver.html in a text editor, then open it using the second way in Step 7 (localhost). You can’t edit the page on the website.

                🧭 The Nothing class · Varied pictures · Keep the flip setting the same for training and driving · Level 2 · You are the teacher · Level 6

              4. Train, then test in the preview Train the model, then hold up one card at a time in the Teachable Machine preview. Every sign should reliably reach 80%, and an empty scene should show Nothing. Try holding something you never taught it and watch the bars. If it doesn’t pass, collect more pictures and train again.

                🧭 Confidence and the threshold · Level 2

              5. Export → Upload my model → copy the link Wait until you get the model’s link, then copy it and keep it safe. ⚠ Anyone with the link can use this model (Google says that during training the example pictures stay on your computer, unless you choose to save the project to Google Drive.)

                🧭 Privacy: the link is public, so we use cards, not people’s faces

              6. Set up the new body Keep the battery switch off. Open ai_driver_car.ino in the Arduino IDE and press Verify first. If there are no errors, press Upload. Close the Serial Monitor window because only one program can use the port at a time. This code always starts by stopping the wheels with drive(0, 0) and it has a watchdog that stops the wheels by itself if it doesn’t hear one of the right letters for more than 1 second.

                🧭 Protocol · Start from stop · Watchdog · Level 8

                See the whole Arduino file ai_driver_car.ino

                This file is very short, so you can read all of it. The pins, the motors and drive() are the same as in Lesson 16. What’s new is reading letters from the USB cable, plus the watchdog.

                // AI Driver car: the web page's AI sends ONE letter over USB serial, the Arduino drives.
// F = forward, L = left, R = right, S = stop. Pins and drive() are the same as lesson 16.
const int L1 = 5, L2 = 6, R1 = 9, R2 = 10;   // L298N IN1, IN2, IN3, IN4 (ENA/ENB jumpers stay on)
const unsigned long WATCHDOG_MS = 1000;      // no good letter for 1 second = stop
unsigned long lastCommand = 0;               // time (ms) of the last good letter

void drive(int left, int right) {            // speeds from -255 to 255
  analogWrite(L1, left  > 0 ? left  : 0);
  analogWrite(L2, left  < 0 ? -left : 0);
  analogWrite(R1, right > 0 ? right : 0);
  analogWrite(R2, right < 0 ? -right : 0);
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(L1, OUTPUT); pinMode(L2, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(R1, OUTPUT); pinMode(R2, OUTPUT);
  drive(0, 0);                               // always start with the wheels stopped
  Serial.begin(9600);                        // must match baudRate: 9600 in the web page
}

void loop() {
  while (Serial.available() > 0) {           // read every letter that has arrived
    char c = Serial.read();
    if      (c == 'F') drive(150, 150);      // forward
    else if (c == 'L') drive(0, 160);        // right wheel only = turn left
    else if (c == 'R') drive(160, 0);        // left wheel only = turn right
    else if (c == 'S') drive(0, 0);          // stop
    else continue;                           // ignore any other byte (it does not feed the watchdog)
    lastCommand = millis();                  // a good letter feeds the watchdog
  }
  if (millis() - lastCommand > WATCHDOG_MS) drive(0, 0);  // lost contact with the AI: stop
}
              7. Open the brain page You can open the AI Driver page in Chrome or Edge in two ways. The easiest way is to open it from the project kit page which has an address starting with https. The browser counts https pages as safe, so it lets them use the port and the camera. You don’t need python at all. The other way is for when you want to open it from files on your computer. A grown-up opens Terminal in the folder with the files and types python3 -m http.server and then opens http://localhost:8000/ai-driver.html in Chrome or Edge. (Double-clicking the file directly might work in Chrome, but this hasn’t been confirmed yet.)

                🧭 The browser only lets safe pages use the port and the camera · Level 8

              8. Connect the loop with the wheels off the ground Put the car on the box, turn the battery switch on and press 1. Connect robot and choose the port from the list. The page waits 2 seconds (the Arduino often restarts at this point), then sends S first. Paste the model link and press 2. Start camera and allow the camera. The AI line will show something like AI: Forward 93% -> F

                🧭 The full loop: sense, think, send, move · Level 0 · Level 8

                See the key parts of the AI Driver page’s code

                Here are some parts of ai-driver.html copied exactly as they appear in the real file. The full file is on the project kit page.

                1. Key numbers, the threshold and the “I’m still here” heartbeat

                const THRESHOLD = 0.8;    // below 80% sure = not trusted = Stop
const HEARTBEAT_MS = 400; // re-send the current letter so the Arduino's 1000 ms watchdog stays fed
const LETTER = { forward: 'F', left: 'L', right: 'R', stop: 'S' };
const key = (name) => name.trim().toLowerCase(); // "Forward " and "forward" both count

                2. The Connect robot button waits 2 seconds, then starts with S

                // Button 1: the browser shows a list of serial ports (only works from a click)
$('btnSerial').onclick = async () => {
  if (!('serial' in navigator)) return say('No Web Serial here. Use Chrome or Edge on a computer.');
  try {
    const port = await navigator.serial.requestPort();
    await port.open({ baudRate: 9600 });    // must match Serial.begin(9600) on the Arduino
    const w = port.writable.getWriter();
    say('Connected. Waiting 2 seconds while the Arduino restarts...');
    await sleep(2000);                      // an Uno usually resets when the port opens
    writer = w;
    await send('S');                        // always begin stopped
    say('Robot connected. Now start the camera.');
  } catch (e) {
    say('Could not connect: ' + (e.message || e));
  }
};

                3. One turn of the loop: sense, think, send the command

                // One turn of the loop: SENSE (camera) -> THINK (AI) -> ACT (send a letter)
async function loop(id) {
  if (id !== runId) return;                          // STOP was pressed
  webcam.update();                                   // SENSE: grab a new frame
  const preds = await model.predict(webcam.canvas);  // THINK: [{className, probability}, ...]
  if (id !== runId) return;                          // STOP was pressed while the AI was thinking
  const top = preds.reduce((a, b) => (b.probability > a.probability ? b : a));
  const sure = top.probability >= THRESHOLD;
  const letter = sure ? (LETTER[key(top.className)] || 'S') : 'S'; // unsure or unknown class = Stop
  // ACT: send only when the decision changes, plus a heartbeat repeat.
  // This loop pauses when the tab is hidden, so heartbeats stop and the Arduino stops itself.
  if (letter !== lastSent || performance.now() - lastSentAt > HEARTBEAT_MS) await send(letter);
  $('ai').textContent = `AI: ${top.className} ${Math.round(top.probability * 100)}%` +
    (sure ? '' : ' (not sure)') + ` -> ${letter}`;
  requestAnimationFrame(() => loop(id));
}

                4. Emergency stop: send S first, then turn off the camera

                // Emergency stop: the button or the Esc key
async function emergencyStop() {
  runId++;                                           // ends the loop
  await send('S');                                   // stop the wheels first
  if (webcam) { webcam.stop(); webcam = null; }      // then switch the camera off
  $('btnCam').disabled = false;
  say('Stopped. Press Start camera to try again.');
}
$('btnStop').onclick = emergencyStop;
document.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => { if (e.key === 'Escape') emergencyStop(); });

Notice that the car rolls on a little after you raise your hand to stop, and notice that you are the one checking the result and changing the hand sign.

                🧭 Latency · Level 4 · Human-in-the-loop · Level 8

              11. Keep experimenting Try one thing at a time, and always try it with the wheels off the ground first.

You can’t edit the page on the website. Threshold · Level 2

              Learn to read the code: seven lines that keep the car safe

              Line in the codeWhat it means
              THRESHOLD = 0.8The decider: the AI must be at least 80% confident, otherwise it sends S (Level 2)
              LETTER[key(top.className)] || 'S'Any class name that isn’t one of these four words, such as Nothing, becomes S
              HEARTBEAT_MS = 400Sends the same letter again every 0.4 seconds as an “I’m still here” heartbeat, only from inside the AI’s loop (Level 8)
              await sleep(2000) then send('S')Waits for the Arduino to restart, then always starts with Stop
              WATCHDOG_MS = 1000The watchdog in the Arduino: if it doesn’t hear a valid letter for more than 1 second, it stops the wheels by itself
              else continue;Any letter other than F L R S is skipped and doesn’t count as an “I’m still here” signal
              emergencyStop()The STOP button and the Esc key send S first, and only then turn off the camera (Level 7)

              ⚠ Safety first

              • Always work with a grown-up
              • Play on the floor only, never on a table
              • Use the low speeds set in the code
              • An adult stays near the battery switch at all times
              • Test with the wheels off the ground first
              • Keep fingers away from the wheels
              • Switch the batteries off before unplugging any wires
              • Never leave the car running without someone watching
              • Batteries: never mix old and new ones, never short-circuit them, and take them out when you have finished playing
              • Use hand signs or cards, not people’s faces
              • No wireless connection in your first project

                    The brain doctor’s cornerIf we compare it with our body, the AI in the browser does a job similar to the brain’s, the USB cable is like a nerve, and the watchdog in the Arduino is like a spinal cord reflex, which can call a stop by itself without waiting for the brain. All of this is only a comparison to help you understand. The real brain is far more complex than this, and many parts work at the same time (see Level 1). Interestingly, our camera is on the computer, not on the car, so the “Check the result” part of the loop is your own eyes. You see the car turn too far and change your hand sign, so this loop runs through you. This is human-in-the-loop, which we met in Lesson 15
                    For parentsThis project uses batteries and motors, so please stay with your child the whole time, be the one who switches the batteries on and off, and be the one who grants the browser permission to use the port and the camera. The project page loads libraries from cdn.jsdelivr.net and loads the model from Google’s servers. Images from the camera are processed in the browser, but the link to an uploaded model is public, so children should teach the AI only with arrow cards or hand signs, and never take pictures of anyone’s face. The files in this kit have not yet been tested with a real car and camera. Please press Verify in the Arduino program first, and make sure all 8 checks of the wheels-off-the-ground test pass every time before putting the car on the floor.

                    Level 10 · The limits of the comparisonA map, not a photo

                    Where it’s similar, where it isn’t

                    All through this lesson, we have borrowed our own bodies as a map to help us understand robots: eyes are like a camera, nerves are like a USB cable, and spinal cord reflexes are like the watchdog in the Arduino. A good map helps you not get lost, but a map is not a photo. It leaves out an enormous amount of detail. So this last level invites you to look at how far the comparison works, and where it stops. The people who know what their own map is missing are the ones who use maps best.

                    Guess first: alike or not alike?

                    Each row is something we have already met in this lesson. For each one, guess whether our body and a robot are alike, partly alike, or not alike at all. You get one guess per row. Once you have guessed, the answer and a short reason will open by themselves. Don’t worry about being wrong, because some rows have kept scientists arguing for years.

                    ● Alike · ◐ Partly alike · ○ Not alike · ✓ Right guess · ✗ Not quite

                    Guessed 0 of 7 rows · Right guesses: 0 of 7

                    Guess first, then the answer will open by itself

                    Keyboard in this table · Tab goes to the show-answer button, then on to the next row · ← → moves between answers in the same row · Enter, Space or the numbers 1 2 3 choose an answer · After you guess, the show-answer button opens and closes the answer

                    🧩 Diagrams are boxes, but the real brain is many loops

                    Robot diagrams usually draw boxes in a row: sense, then think, then act, one box at a time, like people queuing to buy sweets. This is easy to read, and it really did help us build the car in Level 9. But the real brain is messier and cleverer than that.

                    In the brain, many loops work at the same time: the cerebral cortex, the basal ganglia, the cerebellum and the spinal cord, and they all keep talking to each other. When you reach for a glass of water, your eyes are still looking for the glass, your hand has already started reaching, and your brain is still choosing how to hold it. Even the spinal cord can make quick decisions by itself, such as starting to lift your foot away when you step on something sharp, before the brain is fully aware of it (you can read about this in Level 4 but never try it for real)

                    Both of these pictures are still simplified maps. You can see the four-layer diagram compared with the real brain in more detail, with a switch button, in Level 1

                    🤖 A pain sensor is just a number

                    Some robots have sensors that measure pressure or heat. When the value goes above a set limit, the program might tell the arm to pull back, or make a speaker say “Ouch!” It sounds as if it really hurts, but inside there is only a number going up and a rule that a person wrote.

                    Pressure number goes up→Passes the limit a person set→Speaker says “Ouch”

                    There is no evidence yet that today’s robots or AI really feel pain, happiness or fear, even when they are set up to say “Ouch”. Our pain, on the other hand, is a real feeling that warns us to take care of our body quickly. You can see the table comparing the brain with AI in Lesson 15

                    ⚡ 20 watts versus 700 watts

                    The whole brain uses about 20 watts of power, about the same as a small light bulb (Lesson 15 and Lesson 16). But one powerful AI chip can use up to about 700 watts, as much as about 35 brains.

                    The whole brain, about 20 watts🧠
                    1 powerful AI chip, up to about 700 watts

                    700 ÷ 20 = 35 · One chip at full power equals about 35 brains

                    The 700-watt figure is the most the chip can handle. It doesn’t use that much all the time, and this is only a rough comparison. But don’t forget that big AIs are trained on thousands of chips like this at the same time.

                    🧺 Hard things turn out easy, easy things turn out hard

                    In 1988, a robot scientist called Hans Moravec pointed out that getting a computer to win at draughts is easier than getting it to see and move as well as a one-year-old child. This is an observation from people who work with robots every day, not a law of nature. AI has got much better since then, but walking on rough ground, picking up soft things and folding clothes are still hard for robots.

                    Jobs computers have long been good at
                    • Playing draughts and chess
                    • Doing long sums very fast
                    • Remembering huge amounts of information without forgetting
                    Jobs that are easy for people but still hard for robots
                    • Walking on rough ground, over stones and grass
                    • Picking up soft things without squashing them
                    • Folding clothes that are never crumpled the same way twice

                    Part of the reason may be that our bodies have practised these things every day since we were little, so we have forgotten how hard they are (Level 6), and the real world is never exactly the same twice. One piece of cloth can crumple in thousands of ways, while a draughts board has rules that never change.

                    🔍 Questions to carry with you when you see a robot in the news or in a video

                    This lesson doesn’t predict what future robots will be like, because things change very fast. But we can carry good questions with us that work for every robot, whenever it comes out.

                    🎬How many tries did it take?How many times was this clip filmed? If it had to do the task ten times, how many times would it succeed?
                    🕹On its own, or with human help?Does the robot make every decision by itself, or is a person helping to control it?
                    🔀What if things change a little?If you change the object, the colour or the light a little, can it still do the job? (Level 6)
                    ❓What does it do when it’s unsure?Does it stop or ask a person, or does it keep guessing confidently? (Level 7)
                    🛑Who stops the body?If the AI freezes or a cable comes loose, is there something that can stop the motors by itself? (Level 8)
                    ⚡How much power does it use?How often does it need charging, and how much electricity did its training use?
                    🙋If it goes wrong, who is responsible?The people who built it, the people using it, or the people who let it do the job?
                    💬Real feelings or just words?When it says it is happy or hurt, is there any evidence it really feels that, or was it just set up to say so?
                    The brain doctor’s cornerAs a brain doctor, I see ideas flowing both ways. This is my own view as the author. Engineers have learned from the brain: nerve cells inspired the artificial neural networks inside almost every AI today (Lesson 15), and reflexes that can stop without waiting for the big brain help show why robots need a safety layer that is fast and separate from the AI. Brain doctors have learned from robots and AI too. The surprise number (prediction error) that AI researchers came up with to teach computers has helped scientists better understand some dopamine signals in monkeys, although this is still being debated (Level 6). And techniques that helped AI get better at games gave scientists a new idea to test in mice. They found that each dopamine cell seems to predict rewards differently: some more hopefully, others more cautiously. Every time we borrow an idea from the other side, we have to test it again, because a map of one side is not a photograph of the other.

                      RememberComparing the body with a robot is a map, not a photograph. It helps show what each layer does: the thinking layer, the adjusting layer, the stopping layer and the message wires. But robots have no nerve cells, there is no evidence yet that today’s robots really feel pain, and they use energy very differently from us. Knowing where the map stops is just as important as knowing where the two are alike.

                      Our loopAI is the brain and the robot is the body. Joined together, they make a loop that senses, thinks, sends the command, moves and checks the result, with a fast layer guarding against danger and a person in the loop when it is unsure.

                      Build stepWrite four small labels, 🧠 Think, 🎯 Adjust, 🛑 Stop and 📨 Send messages, then stick each one on the matching part of the car from Level 9 (for example Teachable Machine on the web page, the STOP button, the watchdog in the Arduino and the USB cable). You’ll find that our car doesn’t have a fine-adjusting layer at all yet. If you wanted to add one, think about where the line-following sensor from Lesson 16 would fit in the loop. This is just a thinking game on paper. If you build it for real, always get an adult to check it, and test it with the wheels lifted off the ground first.

                      How to review, the robot-loop way

                      Turn on self-test mode and the explanations will be hidden, leaving only the words. Try saying what each one means in your own words first, then tap to see how close you were. This is the same loop as in Level 5 (guess first, look at the real answer, then fix it).

                      Getting it wrong is completely fine. Seeing where your answer is different from the real one is what shows you what to fix. The robots in this lesson get better in the same way.

                      Where are the words you’ve already learned?

                      You can find basic words such as training data, classification, hallucination and human-in-the-loop in the Lesson 15 glossary and sensor, actuator, feedback control, reinforcement learning and embodied AI in the Lesson 16 glossary

                      If these words confuse you in this lesson, go back and look them up. This lesson deliberately doesn’t explain them again, to leave room for the new words.

                      Our loopAll 24 words help explain the same loop: eyes that must be sure enough, a brain that plans ahead in chunks, a wire that keeps saying it is still there, a body with reflexes, and surprise that helps the loop adapt when something unexpected happens, all with a safety layer always watching underneath.

                      Correct: 0 of 12

                      RememberAI is the brain and the robot is the body. Joined together, they become a loop that goes round and round without stopping: sense, think, send the command, move, check the result, then round again. A good robot isn’t the smartest one, but the one that double-checks before believing, stops by itself when it is unsure or loses contact, and asks a person when it meets something it has never seen. Our bodies work in similar loops too, but many loops run at the same time, which makes the body messier and more amazing than any diagram.
